title: Brute-force search
summary: Brute-force search systematically checks all possible candidates against a problem's constraints, guaranteed to find a solution if one exists. Its implementation cost grows proportionally to the number of candidates, which often increases dramatically with problem size (combinatorial explosion). While simple to implement, it becomes impractical for large problem instances, so it is typically used when problem size is limited, when problem-specific heuristics reduce the candidate set, or as a baseline method for benchmarking other algorithms. In cryptography, this technique underlies brute-force attacks that exhaustively check all possible keys.

mechanisms.title: Exhaustive Candidate Enumeration
mechanisms.explanation: The algorithm generates candidates systematically using first/next procedures and validates each against the problem statement. Implementation costs scale with the total number of candidates, which often grows factorially or exponentially with problem size, making it impractical for large instances without heuristics.

mechanisms.title: Search Space Reduction via Heuristics
mechanisms.explanation: Problem-specific heuristics can dramatically reduce the candidate set before exhaustive checking begins. Examples include restricting arrangements (e.g., eight queens puzzle reduces from 64^8 to 64 choose 8 candidates) and reordering candidates by likelihood of validity (e.g., testing smaller divisors first, or bits with higher probability of being 1 first).
